title: The small-Hurst limit of the expected maximum of fractional Brownian motion
shortTitle: How high does a rough random path climb? The small-Hurst limit of the fBm maximum
oneLine: As fractional Brownian motion becomes very rough (Hurst parameter H → 0), √H times its expected maximum on [0, 1] tends to √2, settling a 2022 conjecture; a uniform grid of n points sees half of that maximum once H log n reaches ½.
abstract: Fractional Brownian motion B_H is the standard model of a rough random path, and its Hurst parameter H sets the roughness: small H means a very rough path, as in rough-volatility models where H is around 0.1. Its expected maximum M_H = E sup over [0, 1] of B_H grows like H^(−1/2) as H → 0, and Bisewski, Dębicki and Rolski (2022) conjectured that √H·M_H has a finite positive limit; the known bounds placed it between 1.128 and 1.695. This candidate proves that the limit is √2, with convergence of the rescaled maximum in every L^p and error orders on both sides. More generally, a Gaussian field whose canonical metric is asymptotically d^H on a compact Ahlfors s-regular space has limit √(2s), and every such space carries such fields; for compact Euclidean sets the upper box dimension gives an upper bound. The all-time maximum with linear drift has the same constant. For a uniform grid with n intervals and H log n → c, the sampled maximum times √H tends to an explicit F(c), equal to √c up to c = ½ and then rising to √2, so a grid captures half the continuum mean at c = ½ and all of it only when H log n → ∞; quasi-uniform nets in regular spaces obey √s·F(c/s). The paper also proves M_H ≤ √(3 log 2 / H) for every 0 < H ≤ 1, with a consequent bound for Pickands' constant, and gives numerically evaluated two-sided bounds at fixed H and a Monte Carlo check of the grid law; these show that the first-order formulas converge slowly. Hierarchical Gaussian maxima (GREM/CREM), Gaussian comparison and concentration are classical; the vanishing-exponent limits, the dimension law and the grid crossover are the proposed contribution. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Small-Hurst limit (Theorem 1, proof): lim_{H→0} √H·E sup_{0≤t≤1} B_H(t) = √2, with L^p convergence of √H·sup B_H for every p, and √(2/H) − O(√log(1/H)) ≤ M_H ≤ √(2/H) + O(H^{3/2}); this settles the conjecture of Bisewski, Dębicki and Rolski (2022).

Explicit bounds (Corollary 3 and Lemma 4, proof; Table 1, numerical): M_H ≤ √(3 log 2 / H) for every 0 < H ≤ 1, Pickands' constant H_H ≤ (29.86 H)^{1/(2H)} for 0 < H ≤ ½, and two-sided tree comparisons evaluated numerically (at H = 0.1, M_H lies in about [2.43, 3.50], against √(2/H) = 4.47).

Dimension law (Theorem 5, Corollary 6, Proposition 7, proof): fields with canonical metric asymptotically d^H on a compact Ahlfors s-regular space have limit √(2s) (√(2d) for a cube in R^d); every such space carries such fields; for compact K ⊂ R^d the lim sup is at most √(2·upper box dimension), and Hausdorff dimension does not govern the limit.
Drift (Theorem 8, proof): M_H − 1 ≤ E sup_{t≥0}(B_H(t) − t) ≤ M_H + 4.083 for H ≤ ½, so the all-time maximum with any linear drift has the same constant √2.

Grid law (Theorems 11 and 13, proof; Table 2, Monte Carlo): with H log n → c, √H·E max over the grid {i/n} tends to F(c) = √c for c ≤ ½ and √2(1 − e^{1/2−c}/2) for c ≥ ½, so a grid captures half the continuum mean at c = ½ and 90% at c ≈ 2.11; quasi-uniform nets in Ahlfors s-regular spaces give √s·F(c/s). At H = 0.05–0.2 simulated grid means lie 17–42% below the first-order values.

narration: How high does a rough random path climb? An Evidence Press briefing. Fractional Brownian motion is the standard model of a random path with a tunable roughness, set by a number called the Hurst parameter. When that number is small, the path is extremely jagged. Such paths are used, for example, to model the volatility of financial markets, where the Hurst parameter is often around one tenth. A basic question is how high such a path climbs, on average, over a unit of time. Mathematicians knew that the answer grows like one over the square root of the Hurst parameter, and they had bounds on the constant in front, but not its value. In 2022, Bisewski, Dębicki and Rolski conjectured that a limiting constant exists. This paper proves that it does, and that it is the square root of two. The idea is that a very rough path behaves like a branching tree of independent random choices, and the maximum of such a tree can be computed exactly. The paper also shows how the answer changes in higher dimensions, and it answers a practical question: how finely must you sample a path to see its maximum? A grid sees half of it once the Hurst parameter times the logarithm of the number of points reaches one half, and all of it only as that product grows without limit. So for very rough paths the number of points needed grows exponentially. These are limiting results, and they converge slowly; the paper also gives explicit bounds and numerical tables for realistic values. The proofs are written out in full and checked by scripts. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on the third of November twenty twenty-six, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

relatedWorks.citation: Bisewski, Dębicki and Rolski (2022). Derivative of the expected supremum of fractional Brownian motion at H=1. Queueing Systems. Records the bounds window [1.128, 1.695] and conjectures that the small-Hurst limit exists; Theorem 1 resolves it.

Borovkov, Mishura, Novikov and Zhitlukhin (2018). New and refined bounds for expected maxima of fractional Brownian motion. Statistics & Probability Letters. Source of the upper constant 1.695 and of the Shao-inequality route to Pickands' constant.

Borovkov, Mishura, Novikov and Zhitlukhin (2017). Bounds for expected maxima of Gaussian processes and their discrete approximations. Stochastics. Earlier bounds of the right order and discretisation errors.
Bisewski (2023). Lower bound for the expected supremum of fractional Brownian motion using coupling. Journal of Applied Probability. Source of the lower constant 2/√π ≈ 1.128.

Bisewski, Dębicki and Mandjes (2021). Bounds for expected supremum of fractional Brownian motion with drift. Journal of Applied Probability. The ratio form of the drift limit, sharpened here to an additive bound.

Borovkov and Zhitlukhin (2018). On the maximum of the discretely sampled fractional Brownian motion with small Hurst parameter. Electronic Communications in Probability. Normal limit for grid maxima when H(log n)² → 0, the regime extended by Theorem 11.
Makogin (2016). Simulation paradoxes related to a fractional Brownian motion with small Hurst index. Modern Stochastics: Theory and Applications. Fixed grids miss the maximum at small H.

Bovier and Kurkova (2004). Derrida's generalized random energy models 2: models with continuous hierarchies. Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincaré, Probabilités et Statistiques. The CREM ground-state formula used for the grid law.

Bovier and Kurkova (2004). Derrida's generalised random energy models 1: models with finitely many hierarchies. Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincaré, Probabilités et Statistiques. Finite-level hierarchical maxima.

Addario-Berry and Maillard (2020). The algorithmic hardness threshold for continuous random energy models. Mathematical Statistics and Learning. Same concave-majorant convention; motivates the adaptive-sampling conjecture.
Assouad (1983). Plongements lipschitziens dans R^n. Bulletin de la Société Mathématique de France. The snowflake embedding behind Corollary 6.
Gatheral, Jaisson and Rosenbaum (2018). Volatility is rough. Quantitative Finance. Rough-volatility models with H around 0.1.

Neuman and Rosenbaum (2018). Fractional Brownian motion with zero Hurst parameter: a rough volatility viewpoint. Electronic Communications in Probability. The H → 0 limit in a different normalisation.
Fyodorov, Khoruzhenko and Simm (2016). Fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index H=0 and the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. The Annals of Probability. Log-correlated limit of fBm.

Ding, Roy and Zeitouni (2017). Convergence of the centered maximum of log-correlated Gaussian fields. The Annals of Probability. Maxima of log-correlated fields, also governed by dimension at first order.
Fang and Zeitouni (2012). Slowdown for time inhomogeneous branching Brownian motion. Journal of Statistical Physics. Basis of the conjectured H^(1/6) second-order term.
Davies and Harte (1987). Tests for Hurst effect. Biometrika. Exact circulant-embedding simulation used for Table 2.
Mukeru and Mulaudzi (2026). Mean maximum of fractional Brownian motion. Physical Review E. Conjectured a formula whose 1/H order is incompatible with the known bounds.
Zhang (2026). Boundedness of discounted branching random walks via generic chaining. arXiv:2602.18919. A class containing the comparison trees.

decisionObject.description: The first-order law for the expected maximum of very rough fractional Brownian motion, √(2/H), with the explicit bound √(3 log 2 / H) at every H, numerically evaluated fixed-H brackets, and the grid rule that a uniform grid of n points captures the fraction F(H log n)/√2 of it (half at H log n = ½).
decisionObject.scope: Standard fBm on [0, 1] and Gaussian fields with snowflake metrics on Ahlfors-regular spaces, in the limit H → 0. Fixed-H levels are given only by the bounds and numerical tables; second-order terms, fluctuations and adaptive sampling are not settled.
